chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
title: Success in Europe at age 71 and doubts about the United States
summary: Based in London for three and a half years and booked across the Continent, Freeman says a genuine jazz soloist is valued more as he ages.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I have been so lucky really, in and all the good white players who were later to become famous soloists, were very lucky that they had this music to use because without it, it might have gone into the studios where they would have become old and not wanted. There's a beautiful thing -- I do not think this has been said before, Helen, about becoming a jazz soloist, that if you are real, genuine, the older you become, the more regard the public has for you, and I am seeing that now at the age of 71, living here in Europe, I have never known nor did I ever know that I was this -- I mean I had never known that I was this well known.

I am based here in London and the work I do is all on the Continent. I do Holland, Italy, France, Germany, Switzerland, Ireland, there is no end to the work, if I want to look ahead, if I am going to live another ten years, I will be booked up another ten years. There is no end to the work, as opposed to , and I say with all due respect to the United States, which is certainly a lovely and great country, because they are a great people, I doubt very much that I would have this sort of success in the
United States. But there again, I don't know, because Dexter Gordon the great tenor player, went away all those years, and now he has become an idol in the States.
